newsitem.title: LEBANON: Hizbollah lambasts Lebanon's prime minister.
newsitem.headline: Hizbollah lambasts Lebanon's prime minister.

text.p: Hizbollah accused Lebanon's billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri in a blistering attack of provoking sectarian strife by working to defeat the militant group in the country's month-long parliamentary polls.

The pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God), two of whose eight members in the current 128-member parliament have already lost their seats, leads a guerrilla war against Israeli occupation forces in south Lebanon.

"I accuse the prime minister of being the first conspirator against civil peace in Lebanon...He can't stand an open-minded Islamist group in Lebanon," Hizbollah head Sheikh Hassan Nasrallah told a rally in south Lebanon on Friday.
He was speaking two days before south Lebanon votes in the fourth stage of the five-round polls in which pro-government candidates have so far won a crushing victory.

"There are those in the government who strive to push and corner the Islamists; to push them and force them to present a model other than the one they believe in in Lebanon, so they resort to a situation similar to Algeria or Egypt," he said.
Nasrallah was referring to the Egyptian government's battle against Islamic militants seeking to oust it and the Algerian government's war against Moslem fundamentalist guerrillas.

He said remarks by Hariri, published by the London-based Lebanese daily al-Hayat this week, that Moslem fundamentalism in Lebanon would be finished soon amounted to a declaration of war but Hizbollah would not be sucked into such violence.

Al-Hayat had quoted Hariri, a tycoon spearheading Lebanon's revival from the 1975-90 civil war, as saying: "We have nearly gotten rid of Christian fundamentalism which retreated and only have Moslem fundamentalism...to confront."
"For sure he means Hizbollah," Nasrallah told the rally of 30,000 supporters in the town of Nabatiyeh.
"Isn't this a declaration of war against a major struggling faction in Lebanon? A war in which the state and its organs, money and a huge election machine and big political capability is being used."
He added: "They (officials) are bothered there are Islamists in Lebanon who can not be sucked into violence even if they're stabbed in the back."

Three militants were defeated when Beirut voted last Sunday in the elections while Hariri and 13 supporters were elected. But Hizbollah is expected to win seats in the coming votes in south Lebanon and the Bekaa Valley on the next two Sundays.
